(a) Explain how the statement passes through the major phases of a compiler, from lexical analysis to code

A compiler works in two halves: the analysis (front end) — lexical, syntax and semantic analysis plus intermediate-code

(f) Explain how the grammar establishes precedence of * over +.
The grammar is stratified into levels: E handles + , T handles * , F handles operands and parentheses. An operator introduced
lower (deeper) in the derivation is applied first. Since every + is generated by E′ at the E-level and its operands are whole T’s, a
product id * id must be completely derived inside one T before it can become an operand of + . Thus in id + id * id the
subtree for id * id lies below the + , i.e. id + (id * id) . Parentheses (F → (E)) go back to the top level to override
precedence. Associativity: the right-recursive E′/T′ chains are evaluated left-to-right in the SDT (inherited attributes), giving left
associativity.

(c) Explain how precedence and associativity resolve the conflicts.
 Each operator token gets a precedence level and an associativity: + (level 1, left), * (level 2, left). A production gets the

 Rule: on a conflict between reducing by production p and shifting token a: if prec(a) > prec(p) → shift; if prec(a) < prec(p) →

 This is exactly how YACC handles %left '+' / %left '*' declarations, allowing a small ambiguous grammar to be used
 with an LR parser.

(e) Explain why the grammar is ambiguous.

 A grammar is ambiguous if some string in its language has more than one parse tree (equivalently, more than one leftmost or

(b) Explain short-circuit evaluation.

 In short-circuit (jumping) code, the operators &&, || and ! are not computed as values; they are translated into conditional

 Inside a block control enters only at the top and leaves only at the bottom, so statements execute sequentially without
